SEC24A-01.note: 'larvae' is plural and the habitual 'whenever ... drops' plus the present-tense frame require 'are'. 'were' is attractive to anyone who knows larvae is plural but misses the tense.

SEC24A-02.note: Subject 'pastures' takes 'are'; the agent is the singular 'field vole', so 'it'. 'them' is attractive because plural pastures/plural verb invite a plural pronoun, and 'grass' pulls toward 'is'.

SEC24A-03.note: Head noun 'lining' is singular and 'if the burning returns' sets a present conditional, so 'is examined'. The compound 'esophagus and stomach' right before the blank makes 'are' attractive.

SEC24A-04.note: 'Harvest after harvest' takes a singular verb, and 'some sixty years ago' rules out the present perfect, so 'was'. 'were' tempts readers who hear the repetition as plural; the deciding time phrase sits well past the blank.

SEC24A-05.note: A compound subject joined by 'and' takes 'have', and the pronoun must be the plural 'their'. 'has its own' reads naturally if the solver takes 'rootstock' as the subject.

SEC24A-06.note: The elliptical auxiliary must match the elided 'has appeared', so it is singular 'has', not 'does'. 'does' is the strongest distractor because 'X does too' is the default ellipsis in speech. ('too' marks the ellipsis but does not decide has vs does.)

SEC24A-07.note: 'whether ... had warmed' is an indirect question inside a declarative sentence, so it ends with a period; C is a comma splice and D is a fused sentence. The question mark is attractive because of 'whether'.

SEC24A-08.note: A comma sets off the participial phrase 'leaving a network...' that modifies the main clause; D makes it a fragment and A misattaches it to 'root'. The colon is the strongest distractor, since an independent clause precedes it, but a colon does not introduce a modifying participial phrase.

SEC24B-01.note: The ellipsis stands for 'resist', so the auxiliary is 'do', and the plural 'kinds' gives 'do not'. 'does not' is attracted by 'sandstone'; 'are not' fails because there is no predicate it can stand in for.

SEC24B-02.note: The subject is the singular 'rotor'; the parenthetical list does not count toward it. 'as two engineers watch' sets the present tense. 'are being tested' is pulled by 'three fiberglass blades'.

SEC24B-03.note: Head noun 'measurements' is plural, and 'unless ... is removed' sets a present general condition, so 'are overstating'. 'were overstating' gets number right but tense wrong. This is one of the few items where the noun nearest the blank ('satellites') agrees with the key.

SEC24B-04.note: Head noun 'Samples' is plural, and 'until a supply ship reached' requires the past, so 'were sealed'. 'was sealed' is pulled by 'core', and 'are sealed' is right on number but wrong on tense.

SEC24B-05.note: The singular 'housing' takes 'shields', and the object refers to the plural 'sensors', so 'them'. 'shield them' is pulled by the plural 'girders'/'sensors' next to the blank.

SEC24B-06.note: 'migrated' is a past participle of an intransitive verb, so it needs perfect 'has' (passive 'was migrated' is wrong). The singular subject is 'dune'. 'have' is pulled by 'lake beds'. 'migrated' falls outside the four-word window because of the interrupter, but it settles was vs has; I list it for reference.

SEC24B-07.note: Two independent clauses, with 'within a decade' opening the second, so a semicolon. A is a comma splice and B is fused. The colon is the strongest distractor: it joins the clauses grammatically, but the second clause does not explain the first, so on SAT convention it is not a second key.

SEC24B-08.note: 'ground out ... and refilled' is a compound predicate with one subject, so no comma before 'and'. 'and,' is never right and can be struck on sight. 'seam, and' is the strong lure because a comma before 'and' feels like the clause-joining habit.

SEC24C-01.note: 'Everything' is singular, and the past real conditional ('if ... found') describes a historical rule, so 'was forfeit'. 'were forfeit' is doubly attractive: it matches 'shelves' and looks like a subjunctive. But a subjunctive 'were' would belong in an if-clause, not this main clause.

SEC24C-02.note: Head noun 'practice' is singular, and 'before the railway reached them' is past, which excludes the present perfect. 'were spreading' is pulled by 'cards'.

SEC24C-03.note: 'screens' is plural, and 'when a new owner emptied' fixes the simple past, so 'were removed'. 'have been removed' is right on number but clashes with the past time clause. There is no intervening attractor noun, so the item turns on tense.

SEC24C-04.note: Plural 'pigments' takes 'match', and the comparison needs the plural pronoun 'those' (= the pigments). 'matches that' is pulled by 'copy', and 'match that' is a half-fix.

SEC24C-05.note: The plural 'tablets' take 'are'. The possessive refers to the singular 'shrine', so 'its'. 'are their' is attractive because the plural verb invites a plural pronoun, but 'the tablets are their only record' makes the tablets record themselves.

SEC24C-06.note: A question with the bare verb 'stop' needs do-support, and the singular 'tower' gives 'does the'. 'do the' is pulled by 'towns'. 'is/are' fail only once the solver finds 'stop', which is seven words on.

SEC24C-07.note: An introductory infinitive phrase takes a comma before the main clause 'the volunteers first split'. C makes a fragment, and D ('the,') is garbled and can be struck on sight. B without the comma is a garden path ('transcribe the interviews the volunteers'). Some style guides allow dropping the comma after a short introductory phrase, but here that causes a misreading, so I do not count B as defensible.
SEC24C-07.drop_reason: Too easy for the module-2 hard route: one option ('the,') can be struck on sight, the period option is an obvious fragment, and the comma after an introductory infinitive phrase is an entry-level convention.

SEC24C-08.note: There were three translators, so 'Ruiz' is restrictive (it picks out which translator) and takes no punctuation. Paired commas or paired dashes would wrongly mark it as nonessential; C mixes the marks and can be struck. The commas in A are the strongest lure because appositive names are usually set off.

tells: Nearest-noun heuristic: in most agreement items the noun immediately before the blank disagrees in number with the key (A-02 grass, A-03 stomach, B-01 sandstone, B-02 blades, B-04 core, B-05 girders, B-06 beds, C-01 shelves, C-02 cards, C-04 copy, C-06 towns). A solver who picks the verb NOT agreeing with the nearest noun gets most of them. Exceptions: SEC24B-03 (satellites agrees with key), SEC24A-06 (ragweed agrees), SEC24C-03 and SEC24C-05 (no intervening attractor). The exceptions blunt it, but it still wins about 11 of 15 agreement items.

Tense in the 2x2 grids is always settled by a time clause later in the sentence (ago / until ... reached / before ... reached / when ... emptied / if ... returns / as ... watch / unless ... is removed). A solver who learns 'find the time clause' gets tense for free. But the past/present key split is balanced (is/are: A-01, A-03, B-02, B-03; was/were: A-04, B-04, C-01, C-02, C-03), so this is not a letter or shape tell.

Key letters are perfectly balanced, 6/6/6/6 across 24 items. No mark is always or never the key among the 6 punctuation items (keys: period, comma, semicolon, no comma, comma, no punctuation). Only SEC24B-08 and SEC24C-08 key the plainest option.
No pronoun shape always wins in the verb+pronoun grids (keys: are/it, have/their, shields/them, match/those, are/its; verb-pronoun number matches in 2 and mismatches in 3).
near_duplicates: elliptical auxiliary after a contrast clause, choosing auxiliary type and number
verb number crossed with pronoun number in a 2x2 grid
head noun of an 'of' phrase plus tense set by a later clause
plural subject with tense fixed by a time clause and no attractor
auxiliary choice forced by a later verb form with a plural attractor

phase2_note: All 24 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses) and every authored explanation is coherent. Drop only SEC24C-07, which is too easy. SEC24A-01 is easy but kept, because 'were' (plural but past) makes the solver use the tense rule. The batch-level tell still stands: in about 11 of 15 agreement items the key disagrees with the noun right before the blank. Worth balancing at the batch level.
